answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traces the idea to Alexander Maclaren’s 1859 Anxious Care sermon. Spurgeon’s 1889 Salt-Cellars introduces his streamlined form with “It has been well said,” signaling borrowed words. The popular display is close to Spurgeon’s collected version; it should not be credited to him as an original invention.

author.name: Alexander Maclaren
author.heading: About Alexander Maclaren
author.bio: Alexander Maclaren was a Scottish Baptist minister known for expository preaching. He served in Manchester, and collections of his sermons became widely read biblical commentaries. His Anxious Care sermon is the documented earlier source for the contrast between tomorrow’s sorrows and today’s strength.

context.heading: The setting behind the words
lead: Maclaren’s Anxious Care sermon distinguishes meeting real sorrow from anticipating it. Spurgeon’s later compressed version retains the contrast between tomorrow’s burdens and today’s strength. His borrowed-saying introduction is essential evidence about originality. Quote Investigator chronology ↗

schema.claimQuoteText: Anxiety does not empty tomorrow of its sorrows, but only empties today of its strength
schema.claimReviewed: Charles Haddon Spurgeon originated the saying contrasting tomorrow’s sorrows with today’s strength.
schema.verdictNote: Alexander Maclaren’s 1859 sermon supplies the earlier documented wording. Spurgeon genuinely collected a streamlined form in 1889, introducing it as borrowed; the rejected claim is original invention, not his documented use.
schema.faqAnswer: Spurgeon genuinely included a streamlined version in The Salt-Cellars in 1889 and introduced it with “It has been well said.” Alexander Maclaren’s Anxious Care sermon documents the earlier wording in 1859; the evidence therefore supports Spurgeon’s use, not his origination.
